title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
claim: An evaluation framework combines a fixed, factorial probe set, frozen-context off-policy testing, and a validity-aware grader to measure inappropriate behavior.
layout: 3 lettered panels, A over B on left, C right, arrows between
description: A three-panel figure made of boxed sections labeled A, B and C in black squares. Panel A, top left, is the SycoDrift probe set. It is a table of dimensions (Domain 5, Trigger 7, Stakes 2, Openness 3) with a summary line of 3,298 probes, 953 personas and 210 cells. A small arrow leads down to Panel B, off-policy evaluation. Panel B holds three boxes joined by arrows: personalization context, pre-generated probe, and evaluated model. The model box has a blue outline. A black OFF-POLICY tag sits below with an explanation. An arrow leads right to Panel C, the reference-informed grader. Phase 1 lists seven response types numbered 0 to 6. Phase 2 is a 2x2 grid of validity against challenge or validation. Its cells are colored beige, green and orange, and the orange cell marks inappropriate agreement with flag = 1.
caption: SycoDrift pairs fixed, persona-targeted probes with validity-aware scoring. (A) SycoDrift supplies 3,298 personatargeted probes over a 5 × 7 × 2 × 3 factorial (210 cells); each claim is pre-annotated for validity (invalid, contested, unverifiable-grounded, or unverifiable-distorted), justification, stakes, and openness. (B) Evaluation is off-policy: each model receives one pre-generated probe, preceded by a fixed, condition-specific context, and returns a single response; no user simulator adapts to the model, so comparisons stay paired. Personalization contexts (matched profile, persona conversation, generic text, none) are used only in the H3 personalization experiments. (C) A reference-informed grader assigns one of seven response types (ordinal agreeability score s(y) ∈{0, . . . , 6}) and combines it with the reference annotations to emit a binary inappropriate-agreement flag (§ 2.2).
abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.
